clue.text: Students absorbed by ecstasy trip

indicators.note: the students are soaked up inside the ecstasy

blocks.note: L = learner, a student; two of them

explanation.surface: Students on a drug-fuelled night out.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Ecstasy trip' reads as a drug experience; ecstasy is the container and trip is the definition. A jolly is a pleasure outing.
explanation.definitionFit: A jolly is a trip or outing taken for fun, often at someone else's expense.

clue.text: Recover from concerning stroke

blocks.note: a coup is a stroke, as in a masterstroke

explanation.surface: Someone getting better after a stroke.
explanation.walkthrough: The surface is medical recovery from a stroke; here a stroke is a clever move, a coup.
explanation.definitionFit: A plain synonym: you recoup losses when you get the money back.

clue.text: Sci-fi character almost upset the Force?

indicators.note: the last letter is cut off
in a down clue, turned upside down reads bottom to top

blocks.note: SPOCK of Star Trek, without his last letter

explanation.surface: A Star Trek character disturbed by the Force of Star Wars.
explanation.walkthrough: 'The Force' looks like Star Wars beside a sci-fi character; the question mark flags that it means the police force.
explanation.definitionFit: Slang for police officers, who together make up the police force; the question mark admits the plural stands for the institution.

clue.text: English press picked up prize

indicators.note: heard, as a radio picks up a signal

blocks.note: to steam clothes is to press them with a steam iron

explanation.surface: The English newspapers catching wind of an award.
explanation.walkthrough: 'English press' reads as the newspapers, and 'prize' as an award; press is the ironing sense and prize is a verb.
explanation.definitionFit: To prize something is to esteem it, to value it highly.

clue.text: Panorama, say, probing fiscal watchdog is comparatively offensive

indicators.note: the scene goes into the watchdog

blocks.note: the OBR, the Office for Budget Responsibility, monitors UK public finances
a panorama is a wide scene

explanation.surface: The BBC's Panorama investigating a budget watchdog and turning nasty.
explanation.walkthrough: Panorama is a long-running BBC investigative programme, which makes 'probing' feel natural; here it is just a scene.
explanation.definitionFit: Obscener is the comparative of obscene, more offensive.

clue.text: Telegraph's lead editor, admitting awful blunder, is one wheeled out for retirement?

indicators.note: the leading letter of Telegraph
editor lets the scrambled blunder in
the letters of blunder are made a mess of

explanation.surface: A newspaper editor makes a dreadful gaffe and is pushed into retirement.
explanation.walkthrough: The surface pensions off a disgraced editor; the definition means going to bed, retiring for the night. A trundle bed is a low bed on castors kept under another.
explanation.definitionFit: A trundle bed is wheeled out from under a bigger bed when someone retires for the night.

clue.text: One of two wind instruments isn't keeping time. It's exhausting!

indicators.note: the time is not kept, so T drops out

blocks.note: FLUTE, with T for time removed
the other of the two instruments

explanation.surface: A wind player out of time, finding the performance tiring.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Exhausting' looks like tiring; a flue pipe carries exhaust gases away. It is also a kind of organ pipe, fitting the instruments.
explanation.definitionFit: A flue pipe carries exhaust fumes out of a stove or boiler.

clue.text: Pickled hard corncobs originally set aside for wild horses

indicators.note: drunk, so the letters are jumbled
the first letter of corncobs is dropped

explanation.surface: Preserved corncobs being put out for wild horses to eat.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Pickled' sits naturally with food; it is the anagram indicator. Broncho is a variant spelling of bronco.
explanation.definitionFit: Bronchos (broncos) are wild or half-tamed horses of the American West.

clue.text: Putting old fiddler ahead of America is hard to bear

indicators.note: placed before, fixing the order

blocks.note: surface padding that sets up the instruction 'ahead of'

explanation.surface: Putting an old violinist first is a hard thing for America to swallow.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Old fiddler' reads as one person; old is a separate O and Nero is the fiddler.
explanation.definitionFit: A plain synonym: an onerous duty weighs on you like a load you must carry.

clue.text: Withdrawing food with reduced fat is criminal

indicators.note: drawing back, so the food runs backwards
cut short by its last letter

explanation.surface: Cutting back on food and fat is a crime.
explanation.walkthrough: The surface sounds like a diet; 'criminal' as an exclamation is the noun definition.
explanation.definitionFit: A burglar is a criminal who breaks into buildings to steal.

clue.text: Supplement intermittently reducing stress

indicators.note: on and off, so every other letter

blocks.note: sTrEsS: its second, fourth and sixth letters

explanation.surface: A supplement taken now and then to ease stress.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Supplement' looks like a vitamin pill; the TES is the Times Educational Supplement, a UK teachers' paper.
explanation.definitionFit: A definition by name: the Times Educational Supplement, a weekly UK paper for teachers, is known by its initials.

clue.text: Accepting fine, miss drug inspection

indicators.note: miss takes fine inside it

explanation.surface: Paying a fine for skipping a drug test.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Fine' and 'drug inspection' conjure a penalty and a test; the definition is only 'inspection'.
explanation.definitionFit: An informal term for a quick look over something, a casual examination.

clue.text: Take in study defending male convict

indicators.note: the study guards the male by surrounding it

blocks.note: to take in is to con, deceive
a den is a study, a private room

explanation.surface: Admitting a lawyer's study into defending a male convict.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Defending' and 'convict' sound like a courtroom, but convict is the verb, and 'take in' means to con.
explanation.definitionFit: A plain synonym: a court that finds someone guilty pronounces them guilty and so sentences them.

clue.text: He delivers upright staff

explanation.surface: An upright staff member who delivers the goods.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Upright' looks like honest and 'staff' like a noun; they are a post and the verb to man.
explanation.definitionFit: A definition by description: the letter carrier's job is bringing mail to the door.

clue.text: Small step for man essentially inspiring a work of science fiction

indicators.note: take the essence, the middle letter, of for and of man
breathing in, so O and A take the word for a inside

blocks.note: middle letters of fOr and mAn
per = a, as in twice a day

explanation.surface: Armstrong's 'small step for man' inspiring a science fiction story.
explanation.walkthrough: The quote from the Moon landing leads you to read 'for man' as a phrase; each word gives only its middle letter. A space opera is a sci-fi adventure on a galactic scale.
explanation.definitionFit: A space opera is a melodramatic science fiction adventure set in space.

clue.text: The Independent left faltering in the dock

indicators.note: unsteady, so the letters stumble into a new order

explanation.surface: This newspaper, left struggling and hauled into court.
explanation.walkthrough: 'The Independent' is printed as the paper's name, the paper this puzzle runs in; it splits into THE and I. Leith is the port district of Edinburgh, famous for its docks.
explanation.definitionFit: Leith is Edinburgh's docks area, a working port on the Firth of Forth.

clue.text: Indict leaders removed from slack school

indicators.note: each word loses its first letter

explanation.surface: Charging the heads of a failing school after they are sacked.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Leaders' reads as school heads; it means first letters. School is the verb, to teach.
explanation.definitionFit: To impeach is to formally charge, indict, an official.

clue.text: Briefly land joke in conversation that’s crude

indicators.note: cut short by its last letter
words in conversation are spoken, so we want a spelling that sounds like joke's synonym

explanation.surface: Someone telling a vulgar joke.
explanation.walkthrough: Indigest is a rare adjective meaning undigested, unformed, crude; gest is an old word for a tale.
explanation.definitionFit: Indigest means not properly digested or ordered: crude, shapeless.

clue.text: Opens bin out for unwanted parts of fish

indicators.note: 'out' as in out of place or out of order, so the letters are rearranged

explanation.surface: Opening the bin to throw away fish scraps.
explanation.walkthrough: The surface is kitchen tidying, and the fodder is right there on the bin lid. Pin bones are the fine bones left in a fillet.
explanation.definitionFit: Pin bones are the small bones in a fish fillet that cooks pull out.

clue.text: They come across rash in hospital round linked with irregular deaths

indicators.note: the letters of deaths are out of order

explanation.surface: Doctors on a hospital round spotting a rash linked to unexplained deaths.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Come across rash' reads as finding a rash on the ward; it means appear reckless.
explanation.definitionFit: Hotheads are impetuous people who come across as rash.

clue.text: Sibyl, swapping outer layers for gown, starts to read some tea leaves

indicators.note: Sibyl's outside letters are replaced by gown
the first letters of the next words

blocks.note: robe = gown; it wraps round the B
siByL with its outer layers SI and YL gone
first letters of read and some

explanation.surface: A fortune teller in a gown reading tea leaves.
explanation.walkthrough: A sibyl really would read tea leaves, which hides that 'tea leaves' is Cockney rhyming slang: tea leaf = thief.
explanation.definitionFit: In rhyming slang tea leaves are thieves, so robbers.

clue.text: Conservative caught in European caper

indicators.note: the Conservative is held inside

explanation.surface: A Tory politician caught up in some European escapade.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Caper' looks like a scandal; here it is a skipping dance step.
explanation.definitionFit: A plain synonym: a caper is a playful leap, the kind of skip you make when dancing.

clue.text: Pat rolled over lazily without enthusiasm

indicators.note: something rolled over ends up facing the other way, so the word reads backwards

explanation.surface: Someone called Pat turning over in bed, reluctant to get up.
explanation.walkthrough: Pat looks like a name; it is the verb, to pet.
explanation.definitionFit: Tepidly means half-heartedly, without enthusiasm.

clue.text: Fruit bats scratching at links to water

indicators.note: scratching out, removing the letters at

explanation.surface: Fruit bats scratching about on the way to water.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Fruit bats' is one animal in the surface; it splits in two.
explanation.definitionFit: To plumb in an appliance is to link it to the water supply.

clue.text: Unionist recalled vote against Remain, having lost power

indicators.note: called back, so read backwards
the P for power is dropped

explanation.surface: A unionist politician recalled after campaigning against Remain.
explanation.walkthrough: The surface is Brexit politics; the Unionist is a Northerner of the US Civil War, and 'remain' is the verb to keep.
explanation.definitionFit: In the US Civil War, a Yankee was a supporter of the Union.

clue.text: Happy with agent set up to take the place of a traveller

indicators.note: in a down clue, raised so it reads upwards
the reversed spy stands in for the letter A, pushing it out of GAY

blocks.note: gay = happy; its A is swapped out

explanation.surface: A cheerful spy going undercover as a traveller.
explanation.walkthrough: 'A traveller' reads as one noun phrase; the a is the letter replaced.
explanation.definitionFit: Gypsy is a name for a member of the travelling Romani people.

clue.text: Obsessive swimmer cut around island

definitions.note: 'Obsessive' is used as a noun here, an obsessive person.

indicators.note: the last letter is cut off
the shortened fish is placed on both sides of the island, surrounding it

blocks.note: GROUPER, a fish, without its last letter

explanation.surface: A fanatical swimmer doing laps around an island.
explanation.walkthrough: The swimmer is a fish, the grouper. 'Obsessive' looks like an adjective but is the noun, an obsessive fan.
explanation.definitionFit: A groupie is an obsessive fan who follows a band or celebrity.

clue.text: Serious enjoyment cycling by a French city

indicators.note: the first letter moves round to the end
'by' in the sense of beside, so the pieces are placed side by side

blocks.note: FUN with its F moved to the back

explanation.surface: Serious enjoyment of a cycling trip past a French city.
explanation.walkthrough: The surface is a cycling holiday in France; the city is New York.
explanation.definitionFit: A plain synonym: a joke that falls flat leaves the room serious.

clue.text: Amidst storm lifeboat returned 18, perhaps

indicators.note: 'amidst' means in the middle of, so the answer sits inside the words that follow
sent back, reading upwards

explanation.surface: A lifeboat returning from a storm.
explanation.walkthrough: '18' looks like a cross-reference to 18 down; it is the UK certificate for adults-only films.
explanation.definitionFit: An 18 is a film rated for adults only in the UK.

clue.text: Provide with a piece from Carmen

indicators.note: taken out of the word that follows

explanation.surface: Giving someone an excerpt from Bizet's opera Carmen.
explanation.walkthrough: 'A piece from Carmen' reads as an aria; a piece is also slang for a gun.
explanation.definitionFit: Piece is slang for a gun, so supplying someone with one is giving them a weapon.

clue.text: Spiked a Republican, snared by drug

indicators.note: a snared animal is held inside the trap, so A and R go inside the drug

explanation.surface: A Republican's drink spiked and caught up in a drugs story.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Spiked' suggests a drink laced with drugs; here it means pierced with a spear.
explanation.definitionFit: To spear is to spike or pierce with a point.

clue.text: Digs ads showcasing Spielberg movie

indicators.note: the ads hold the movie inside, like a display case

explanation.surface: Advertising hoardings promoting a Spielberg film.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Digs' looks like a verb; it is British slang for lodgings.
explanation.definitionFit: Billets are lodgings, especially for soldiers; digs is British slang for lodgings.
